design_detail: Cross-sectional PET study (Neuropsychopharmacology 2012;37:1465-1473) at Columbia University comparing presynaptic serotonin transporter binding ([11C]DASB) and postsynaptic 5-HT2A receptor binding ([11C]MDL 100907) in 13 people who used ecstasy regularly and 13 matched people who did not. Both scans were acquired, where possible on the same day, with arterial input functions and a two-tissue compartment model; binding potential (BPND) was compared in 17 regions drawn on each person's MRI, with a linear mixed model across all regions, cortical regions and subcortical regions, and a voxel-wise analysis for confirmation.
can_establish: That in this sample, after at least 2 weeks of monitored abstinence, transporter binding was lower and 5-HT2A receptor binding higher in the ecstasy group across cortical regions but not subcortical ones, that the two changes were largest in the same regions, and that non-specific binding (cerebellar distribution volume) did not differ, so the comparison is not an artefact of tracer delivery.
cannot_establish: That ecstasy caused either difference (cross-sectional, 13 people per group, other drug use allowed); that the percentage reductions are meaningful in cortex, where binding in both groups is near zero; that abstinence restores binding (no relation with length of abstinence, in a sample with a narrow range); or that the changes mean loss of terminals rather than lower transporter expression, as the authors state.

sample.recruitment: Not described beyond approval by the New York State Psychiatric Institute review board and written informed consent; diagnoses assessed with the PRISM and/or SCID (Subjects and Methods, 1st-3rd paragraphs).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Ecstasy group: at least 15 lifetime uses and regular use for at least 12 months before enrollment; occasional use of other drugs permitted; 2 weeks' abstinence from all drugs before scanning, monitored twice weekly by urine toxicology and confirmed on the scan day; use in the previous 3 months confirmed by hair analysis. Excluded: any other lifetime Axis I disorder, current substance abuse or dependence other than alcohol or nicotine, past cannabis abuse permitted. Comparison group: same criteria, no Axis I diagnoses and no substance abuse or dependence (Subjects and Methods, 2nd-3rd paragraphs).
sample.demographics: Ecstasy group: 8 men, 5 women, mean age 30.8 (SD 3.8); [11C]DASB comparison group 8 men, 5 women, 27.3 (7.5), p=0.15; [11C]MDL comparison group 9 men, 4 women, 31.1 (10.1). Both groups predominantly white (Table 1).
sample.attrition: Fourteen people who used ecstasy were recruited; one was excluded after the scans because of a technical problem during the receptor scan, leaving 13. Eighteen comparison participants were scanned, of whom 8 had both tracers and 5 had only one; 13 were matched to the ecstasy group for each tracer (Results, 1st paragraph; Table 1 footnote).
sample.selection_effects: A small volunteer sample with a decade of ecstasy use and no psychiatric disorder, which the authors say is hard to find without other drug use; people who develop problems or who use other drugs heavily are excluded by design.

exposure.measurement: Self-report assessed with the PRISM and/or SCID; twice-weekly urine toxicology during the 2-week abstinence and on the scan day; hair analysis confirming use in the previous 3 months (Subjects and Methods, 2nd paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Lifetime sessions mean 142, median 50, range 15-1050; duration of use mean 93 months, median 84, range 4-216; frequency mean 1.9 sessions a month, median 0.8, range 0.3-6.3. Doses per session are not reported (Results, 2nd paragraph).
exposure.polysubstance: All 13 used alcohol regularly and 2 met criteria for alcohol abuse or dependence; 10 of 13 used cannabis regularly; 6 were smokers; 5 had more than 10 lifetime exposures to hallucinogens; more than 10 lifetime exposures to cocaine in 1, ketamine 1, amphetamine 3, opiates 1 (Results, 3rd paragraph). The authors discuss that lower binding has been reported in people who use methamphetamine and that 3 of their participants had used amphetamine (Discussion, 3rd paragraph).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: At least 2 weeks monitored; mean 5.7 weeks, median 8, range 2-8 weeks (Results, 2nd paragraph).

comparison.controls: Healthy people matched by age, ethnicity and gender, with no DSM-IV Axis I diagnosis and no substance abuse or dependence (Subjects and Methods, 3rd paragraph).
comparison.matching: Matched on age, ethnicity and gender; not matched on cannabis, alcohol or tobacco use, which were much higher in the ecstasy group (6 smokers versus 1).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No pre-use measurement; the authors note that lower cortical serotonin function could predispose to use and that their design cannot refute this (Discussion, 5th paragraph).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Excluded for any substance abuse or dependence; only one was a smoker.

outcomes.instruments: [11C]DASB (100-min scan) and [11C]MDL 100907 (90-min scan) PET on an ECAT EXACT HR+, with arterial input functions, two-tissue compartment modelling and BPND as outcome; regions drawn on each person's MRI by published criteria; simplified reference tissue analysis as a check; voxel-wise confirmation with 12-mm smoothing (Subjects and Methods, 4th-7th paragraphs).
outcomes.validity_norms: Both tracers are selective; the authors note that cortical transporter binding is very low, so the specific signal is small, and that no group difference in cerebellar distribution volume validates the use of BPND. No normative values.
outcomes.operationalization: Presynaptic integrity as transporter BPND; postsynaptic adaptation as 5-HT2A BPND; the hypothesis is a fall in the first and a rise in the second.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None applied to the 17 regional comparisons per tracer; the authors state that no pairwise regional comparison survives correction for multiple comparisons and rest their conclusion on the mixed model (Results, 6th and 9th paragraphs).

analysis.effect_sizes: Transporter binding: lower in the ecstasy group across all regions (F=27.07, p<0.001) and across cortical regions (F=25.65, p<0.001), not subcortical (F=1.99, p=0.16), with no region-by-group interaction. Regional BPND (ecstasy versus comparison group, Table 1): occipital -0.01 (SD 0.08) versus 0.10 (0.11), p=0.01; medial prefrontal 0.07 (0.05) versus 0.13 (0.08), p=0.04; temporal 0.07 (0.09) versus 0.15 (0.09), p=0.04; parietal 0.00 (0.05) versus 0.04 (0.07), p=0.09; dorsolateral prefrontal 0.01 (0.06) versus 0.06 (0.09), p=0.16; caudate 0.77 (0.18) versus 0.77 (0.15), p=0.99; putamen 1.21 (0.33) versus 1.19 (0.16), p=0.86; thalamus 0.94 (0.22) versus 0.99 (0.15), p=0.53; midbrain 1.97 (0.56) versus 1.95 (0.39), p=0.92; hippocampus 0.31 (0.15) versus 0.32 (0.09), p=0.97. Editors' calculation from the printed means and SDs (Hedges g with 95% interval): occipital -1.11 (-1.98 to -0.31), medial prefrontal -0.87 (-1.71 to -0.09), temporal -0.86 (-1.70 to -0.08), thalamus -0.26 (-1.04 to 0.51), hippocampus -0.08 (-0.85 to 0.69), caudate 0.00 (-0.77 to 0.77). 5-HT2A receptor binding: higher across all regions (F=12.73, p<0.001), cortical (F=14.55, p<0.001) and subcortical (F=7.38, p=0.007); dorsolateral prefrontal 2.48 (0.47) versus 2.13 (0.33), p=0.04 (editors' calculation g 0.83, 0.06 to 1.67); parietal 2.38 (0.49) versus 2.00 (0.38), p=0.03 (g 0.84, 0.06 to 1.67). Across the seven cortical regions, the size of the receptor difference tracked the size of the transporter difference (r2=0.54, p=0.057). Correlations with use: dorsolateral prefrontal and parietal transporter binding with lifetime uses r=-0.46 (p=0.12) and -0.46 (p=0.11); with duration of use, occipital r=-0.47 (p=0.12) and parietal -0.44 (p=0.14); none significant, and none with duration of abstinence.
analysis.covariates: None reported; no adjustment for smoking, cannabis or alcohol.
analysis.selective_reporting: All 17 regions are tabulated for both tracers, including the null subcortical results and the non-significant correlations.
analysis.power: Not reported; the authors list the small sample as a weakness and note that the narrow range of abstinence may explain the absence of a relation with abstinence (Discussion, 3rd and 8th paragraphs).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 13 people with about 8 years of ecstasy use and 2 to 8 weeks of monitored abstinence, cortical transporter binding was lower and cortical 5-HT2A binding higher than in 13 matched people, with subcortical transporter binding unchanged; no regional comparison survives correction, and the two changes were largest in the same regions.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract states that, in light of the animal literature, 'the most parsimonious interpretation' is that repeated exposure in humans, even in moderate amounts, 'leads to damage in 5-HT neuron terminals innervating the cortex'. The data are a cross-sectional difference in two binding measures in 13 people; the Discussion itself says that PET cannot determine whether lower binding is loss of terminals or down-regulation, and that a predisposing difference cannot be refuted.

timeline.event: First [11C]DASB study with the same cortical pattern
Largest [11C]DASB study, same cortical pattern, normal striatum
Study with the same tracer finding cortical and some subcortical reductions and no 5-HT2A difference with a different receptor tracer
No difference in men abstinent at least a year, with no current-use group for comparison
Review notes that the very large percentage reductions reported here follow from near-zero cortical binding values

replication.where_it_stands: The fifth of five [11C]DASB studies in people currently using ecstasy to find lower cortical binding, as the paper's own Table 2 sets out; its 5-HT2A finding is the opposite of the altanserin result in the Copenhagen study, which the authors attribute to more hallucinogen use in that sample.

funding.funder: National Institute on Drug Abuse grant R01 DA015806-02; the work was carried out at the New York State Psychiatric Institute and Columbia University Medical Center (Acknowledgments).
funding.declared_conflicts: Declared in full: five authors report no support beyond their employers; others report consultancy or research support from ONO, Sunovion, Lilly, Amgen, Pfizer, GlaxoSmithKline, Pierre Fabre, Bristol-Myers Squibb-Otsuka, Boehringer-Ingelheim, Lundbeck, Otsuka, Shire, Merck and Forest (Acknowledgments).
funding.affiliations_note: Columbia University; no author is from the Baltimore or Toronto groups whose results are being confirmed.

what_would_settle_it: A longitudinal study of the same people during use and after long abstinence, with both tracers and a comparison group matched on cannabis, alcohol and tobacco, large enough that regional differences survive correction.

domains.note: The ecstasy group drank, smoked and used cannabis far more; no covariates were used, and the groups are too small for adjustment.
Hair analysis confirms recent use and urine confirms abstinence, but lifetime sessions are self-reported and range from 15 to 1050, and doses per session are not reported.
Thirteen volunteers with a decade of use and no psychiatric disorder, compared with people screened to have no substance problems; no pre-use measurement.
One participant excluded for a technical failure; the control group differs in composition between the two tracers, which the table footnote states.

Fully quantitative PET with arterial input and two selective tracers; cortical transporter binding is near zero in both groups, so the measure has little room and percentage changes are uninformative.
All regions reported, but 34 regional comparisons without correction; the paper states that none of the regional differences survives correction.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A small, technically careful study whose group difference is robust at the level of the mixed model but not at the level of any single region. It can be cited for the cortical pattern of lower transporter and higher 5-HT2A binding, and for the absence of subcortical differences, not for causation, for a quantitative size of the cortical reduction, or for the absence of a relation with abstinence.

key_findings.finding: Transporter binding was lower in the ecstasy group over all regions (F=27.07, p<0.001) and over cortical regions (F=25.65, p<0.001), but not over subcortical regions (F=1.99, p=0.16), with no region-by-group interaction.

Region by region, binding was significantly lower in occipital (-0.01 vs 0.10, p=0.01), medial prefrontal (0.07 vs 0.13, p=0.04) and temporal cortex (0.07 vs 0.15, p=0.04), and no regional comparison survived correction for multiple comparisons; in several cortical regions the ecstasy group's specific binding could not be detected at all.
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation from the printed means and SDs (Hedges g, 95% interval): occipital -1.11 (-1.98 to -0.31), medial prefrontal -0.87 (-1.71 to -0.09), temporal -0.86 (-1.70 to -0.08).

key_findings.finding: Subcortical binding was the same in both groups: caudate 0.77 vs 0.77 (p=0.99), putamen 1.21 vs 1.19 (p=0.86), thalamus 0.94 vs 0.99 (p=0.53), midbrain 1.97 vs 1.95 (p=0.92), hippocampus 0.31 vs 0.32 (p=0.97).
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: thalamus g -0.26 (-1.04 to 0.51), hippocampus -0.08 (-0.85 to 0.69), caudate 0.00 (-0.77 to 0.77); the intervals are wide, so these nulls bound rather than exclude a difference.

key_findings.finding: 5-HT2A receptor binding was higher in the ecstasy group over all regions (F=12.73, p<0.001), cortical (F=14.55, p<0.001) and subcortical (F=7.38, p=0.007), reaching significance region by region in dorsolateral prefrontal (2.48 vs 2.13, p=0.04) and parietal cortex (2.38 vs 2.00, p=0.03), neither surviving correction.
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: dorsolateral prefrontal g 0.83 (0.06 to 1.67), parietal 0.84 (0.06 to 1.67).

key_findings.finding: Across the seven cortical regions, the regions with the largest fall in transporter binding had the largest rise in 5-HT2A binding (r2=0.54, p=0.057, 5 degrees of freedom); the two medial regions changed least on both measures.
key_findings.locator: Results, 10th paragraph; Figure 4 and its caption

key_findings.finding: No correlation between binding and any use variable reached significance, including duration of abstinence; the closest were transporter binding with lifetime uses in dorsolateral prefrontal and parietal cortex (both r=-0.46, p=0.12 and 0.11) and with duration of use in occipital (-0.47, p=0.12) and parietal cortex (-0.44, p=0.14).

Cerebellar distribution volume did not differ between groups for either tracer (9.7 vs 10.1 ml/g, p=0.63; 19.2 vs 20.4, p=0.46), which the authors give as validation of using BPND for a between-group comparison.

The ecstasy group reported a mean of 142 lifetime sessions (median 50, range 15-1050) over a mean of 93 months (median 84), at 1.9 sessions a month, and had been abstinent 5.7 weeks on average (median 8, range 2-8).

The paper's own summary of the five [11C]DASB studies in people currently using ecstasy records lower cortical binding in all five, unchanged striatum in four of five and unchanged midbrain in all five, with the only study of people who had stopped (12 men) showing no difference anywhere.

reporting_issues.issue: The accounting of the comparison group does not add up: 18 people were scanned, 8 with both tracers and 5 with only one, which is 13, yet 13 are reported for each tracer and the footnote says five in each control group differed between tracers.
reporting_issues.consequence: The identity of the 13 controls per tracer, and what became of the remaining 5 of the 18, cannot be reconstructed from the paper; the two tracer comparisons are not independent, since 8 people appear in both.

reporting_issues.issue: Cortical transporter binding potentials are at or below zero in the ecstasy group (occipital -0.01, orbitofrontal 0.00, parietal 0.00), so percentage reductions computed from them are not interpretable.
reporting_issues.consequence: The 2016 review that tabulates this study reports reductions of 83% to 100% in these regions from exactly these values; the absolute differences (0.04 to 0.11 binding-potential units) are the only interpretable statement.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion attributes the original finding of a large global reduction to a 1995 methods paper on the radiotracer rather than to the 1998 study that reported it.
reporting_issues.consequence: A citation error; the finding in question is McCann et al. (1998), which the same paragraph cites correctly earlier.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract's conclusion that the most parsimonious interpretation is damage to cortical serotonin terminals is stronger than the Discussion, which states that PET cannot distinguish terminal loss from down-regulation and that a predisposing difference cannot be refuted.
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract is the part most often cited; its causal reading is not supported by the design.

reporting_issues.issue: Thirty-four regional comparisons are reported without correction, and the paper says none survives it, yet the regional results are presented in the abstract as significant differences in cortical regions.
reporting_issues.consequence: The mixed-model result is the defensible finding; individual regional p-values of 0.03 to 0.04 should not be quoted as established.
